newsitem.title: USA: UAW, GM reach tentative pact at Grand Rapids plant.
newsitem.headline: UAW, GM reach tentative pact at Grand Rapids plant.

text.p: United Auto Workers and General Motors negotiators reached a tentative deal at a metal stamping plant in Grand Rapids, Mich., Friday, nearly a week after the union's first strike deadline, a GM spokesman said.
Production at the plant had continued after the union extended the deadline on an hourly basis.
The 2,346 members of United Auto Workers union Local 730 are to vote on the deal sometime next week. A previous tentative contract agreement was narrowly defeated last fall.

GM spokesman Peter Ternes said terms of the contract would not be released until they had been ratified. He said the agreement came after 16 hours of negotiations Thursday that resumed at 8 a.m. EDT Friday.
"We believe it's a competitive operating agreement that allows us to continue to provide our customers with high quality parts," Ternes said.
A union spokesman, who declined to be named, said leaders were pleased with the outcome. UAW officials previously said major issues in the dispute included staffing and grievances.

Ternes said the Grand Rapids facility was one of GM's most productive stamping plants. It makes door panels, floor pans, quarter panel parts, roofs and lid assemblies for a variety of GM passenger cars.
The Grand Rapids settlement brings to a close a busy week for UAW and GM negotiators. The UAW set three strike deadlines for parts plants in Wisconsin and Michigan.

On Tuesday, June 17, UAW Local 1866 and GM reached a tentative contract deal for 870 workers at a Delphi Energy & Engine Management Systems plant in suburban Milwaukee, Wis., that makes catalytic converters.
On Friday, June 13, an agreement was reached with UAW Local 455 for 900 workers at a foundry in Saginaw, Mich. Each of the agreements were reached without a work stoppage.
Some analysts had seen the deadlines as the union's way of putting pressure to resolve a two-month-old strike by 5,800 workers at GM's Pontiac, Mich., full-size pickup truck plant.

Talks continued this week to settle the strike, but union officials have said progress was slow. Union officials are demanding that GM add jobs at the plant to ease overtime strains. But the company says a new generation of pickup truck it plans to build there requires some 30 percent fewer workers.
GM said last month strikes at Oklahoma City, Okla., and Pontiac had cost it $225 million in lost profits. GM lost $1.2 billion in earnings to strikes in 1996.
